title: The arms of Hephaestus delivered
greek: τὰ δ᾽ ἀνέβραχε δαίδαλα πάντα (ta d’ anebrache daidala panta)
short: Thetis lays down the god-made armour; it clangs, the Myrmidons cannot bear to look, and Achilles' fury only grows.
body: The opening lines of Book XIX close the episode of the Making of the Arms (the hoplopoiia, Il. 18.369-617), and Leaf thought the book division would have fallen more naturally after line 39. The armour is described as daidala, intricately worked, the word used for Hephaestus' craftsmanship throughout Book XVIII. Its effect is double: the Myrmidons tremble and look away, while Achilles, seeing it, feels his anger (cholos) rise and his eyes flash 'as it had been flame'. The scene sets up two later moments: Achilles' arming in this book (19.364-91), and the duel with Aeneas in Book XX, where the narrator remarks that the gifts of the gods are not easily broken by mortals (20.264-72). The new armour also matters because Hector is now wearing Achilles' old set, stripped from Patroclus (17.194-7), so that in Book XXII Achilles will be fighting, in effect, his own image.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XIX, p. 317
Homer, Iliad 18.369-617 and 19.1-39 (Greek text ed. A. T. Murray, Loeb, 1924)

title: Flies and the defilement of the corpse
greek: μυῖαι … ἀεικίσσωσι δὲ νεκρόν (muiai … aeikissōsi de nekron)
short: Achilles fears that flies and worms will disfigure Patroclus' body while he fights: the first sounding of the poem's theme of the outraged corpse.
body: Achilles' worry is concrete and physical: flies will settle in the bronze-made wounds, breed worms and 'work shame upon' (aeikizein) the body. The verb belongs to the vocabulary of aikia, the deliberate or accidental disfigurement of the dead, which runs from the proem's bodies left for dogs and birds (1.4-5) to Achilles' own treatment of Hector (22.395-404). The irony is pointed: the hero who here cannot bear the thought of his friend's corpse being spoiled will soon try to spoil Hector's, and the gods will then do for Hector exactly what Thetis does for Patroclus, keeping the body whole (23.184-91; 24.18-21, 411-23). Charles Segal's monograph traces this motif through the whole poem and argues that it measures how far the warriors' violence breaks the limits of the human community. Thetis' answer (19.29-33), that the flesh will stay sound for a full year, prepares the next note.

sources.cite: Charles Segal, The Theme of the Mutilation of the Corpse in the Iliad (Mnemosyne Supplement 17, Leiden: Brill, 1971)
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 19.24-39

title: Ambrosia and nectar as preservatives
greek: ἀμβροσίην καὶ νέκταρ ἐρυθρὸν στάξε κατὰ ῥινῶν (ambrosiēn kai nektar eruthron staxe kata rhinōn)
short: Thetis drips the gods' food and drink into Patroclus' nostrils so that his body will not decay: a divine embalming.
body: Ambrosia and nectar are the food and drink of the immortals; applied to a mortal body they keep it from corruption, as Apollo anoints Sarpedon's body with ambrosia (16.670, 680) and Aphrodite anoints Hector's (23.186-7). The detail of the nostrils struck ancient and modern readers as strangely technical. Leaf records Heyne's suggestion that it reflects knowledge of Egyptian embalming, comparing Herodotus 2.86, where the embalmers draw out the brain through the nostrils and pour in drugs; Eustathius, Leaf notes, tried to derive the phrase from a word for hide instead, which Leaf calls a scholiastic masterpiece. Leaf also suggests that nectar is called 'red' (eruthron) because it takes the place of blood. Later in the book Athena drops the same substances into the living Achilles to keep off hunger (19.347-54): the hero who refuses to eat is fed like a corpse or a god.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 19.38
Herodotus, Histories 2.86 (Egyptian embalming)

title: Renouncing the mēnis
greek: μῆνιν ἀποειπών (mēnin apoeipōn)
short: Thetis tells Achilles to 'unsay' his wrath; he does so in a few lines, and the anger that began the poem is formally ended.
body: The phrase is literally 'speaking off the mēnis', the word for the cosmic, god-like wrath announced in the first line of the poem. Achilles renounces it in the assembly with striking brevity (19.67-8: it does not befit him to be angry for ever), and the Achaeans rejoice that the son of Peleus has 'unsaid' it (19.75). The reconciliation is formal rather than emotional: Achilles is indifferent to the gifts (19.147-50) and wants only to fight. His anger is not extinguished but redirected at Hector and the Trojans, and at the arming he is described as in fierce rage against them (19.367). Leonard Muellner's study of mēnis argues that the word is reserved for an anger that threatens cosmic order, and its renunciation here marks the end of the plot of the quarrel. Leaf, from the older analytical standpoint, asked whether any reconciliation scene belonged to the original poem at all.

sources.cite: Leonard Muellner, The Anger of Achilles: Mênis in Greek Epic (Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1996)
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), Introduction to Book XIX, p. 317

title: Helmsmen and stewards at the assembly
greek: κυβερνῆται … οἰήια … ταμίαι, σίτοιο δοτῆρες (kubernētai … oiēia … tamiai, sitoio dotēres)
short: Even the non-combatants, the pilots and the food stewards who never attend assemblies, come to hear Achilles: a measure of the occasion.
body: The Achaean camp includes men who do not fight: helmsmen (kubernētai) who handle the steering-oars (oiēia, a word found only here in the Iliad) at sea, and stewards (tamiai), 'givers of food', who manage supplies on shore. Their presence shows that Achilles' return is an event for the whole army. Leaf, with dry humour, observes that the poet of this book seems determined that the commissariat should not lack its bard, and links the detail to the book's unusual interest in eating and drinking, which dominates the debate at 19.154-237. Readers who do not share Leaf's view that this interest is a mark of late composition can see it as deliberate: the stewards' presence anticipates Odysseus' insistence that the army must eat before battle. Leaf also notes that Zeus is later called the tamiēs of war (19.224), perhaps in pointed contrast with these stewards of bread.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 19.43-44 and 19.224; Introduction to Book XIX, pp. 317-18
Liddell-Scott-Jones, Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. οἰήιον, ταμίας

title: The wounded leaders: Diomedes, Odysseus, Agamemnon
greek: σκάζοντε (skazonte)
short: Diomedes and Odysseus limp in on their spears and Agamemnon arrives last, all still suffering from the wounds of Book XI.
body: The three kings were all wounded on the same day, in Book XI: Agamemnon in the arm by Coon, son of Antenor, whom he then killed (11.248-63); Diomedes in the foot by an arrow of Paris (11.369-78); Odysseus in the side by Socus (11.434-8). Their entrance, leaning on spears, is a visual reminder of the cost of Achilles' absence. Leaf points out that only Diomedes' limp is strictly explained by his wound, and that the next day both he and Odysseus compete in the funeral games (Book XXIII), commenting that the rapid healing of wounds is a privilege of the heroic age. Agamemnon's late arrival and his wound matter for the following scene, in which he speaks without coming forward (19.76-7). Coon is named here only to recall that earlier fight; he has already died.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 19.47 and 19.53

anchor: for the sake of a girl
title: 'For the sake of a girl': Achilles' bitter retrospect
greek: εἵνεκα κούρης (heineka kourēs)
short: Achilles now reduces the cause of the quarrel to 'a girl', and wishes Artemis had shot Briseis on the day he captured her.
body: Achilles opens with a sharply ironic question, 'was this then the better for us twain?', which Leaf reads as bitter rather than conciliatory. The phrase 'for the sake of a girl' shrinks Briseis, whom he called his beloved wife in Book IX (9.336, 342-3), to a mere pretext; the wish that Artemis had killed her with an arrow draws on Artemis' role as sender of sudden death to women (compare 6.428; Od. 11.171-3), just as Apollo's arrows kill men. The cost is spelled out: many Achaeans have 'bitten the vast earth' (a formula for dying men) because of his wrath. The mention of Lyrnessus, the city from which Briseis was taken (2.688-93), connects with her own lament later in the book (19.291-6), where we hear her side of the same event. The contrast between Achilles' dismissive words and Briseis' grief is one of the book's sharpest juxtapositions.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 19.56

anchor: not standing forth in their midst
title: Agamemnon speaks from his seat
greek: αὐτόθεν ἐξ ἕδρης, οὐδ᾽ ἐν μέσσοισιν ἀναστάς (autothen ex hedrēs, oud’ en messoisin anastas)
short: A famous crux: Agamemnon addresses the assembly without rising and coming forward, and his opening words about interruption have been read in several ways.
body: In a Homeric assembly the speaker normally stands in the middle and holds the sceptre (compare 1.245-6, 2.100-9). Agamemnon does not, and his first words, that it is right to listen to a man who stands and not to interrupt him, have puzzled readers since antiquity. Leaf sets out the main lines. If line 77 is taken at face value, Agamemnon excuses himself for speaking seated because of his wound, though his wound is in the arm and would not stop him standing; the scholia assert that Aristarchus supported this view, though Leaf finds it hard to believe. Or 'him who is standing' simply means 'the man on his feet', and Agamemnon is asking for a hearing in a noisy crowd. Leaf also notes a third possibility, that he stood up where he sat instead of going to the centre. Whatever the reading, the posture fits a speech in which the king avoids full responsibility, and contrasts with Achilles, who rose (19.55).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 19.77 and 19.79-80 (citing Lendrum, Classical Review 4, p. 47)
Homer, Iliad 19.76-84 (Greek)

title: 'Not I, but Zeus and Fate and Erinys': Agamemnon's apology
greek: Ζεὺς καὶ Μοῖρα καὶ ἠεροφοῖτις Ἐρινύς (Zeus kai Moira kai ēerophoitis Erinys)
short: Agamemnon blames divine powers for the 'wild blindness' (atē) that made him seize Briseis, yet still offers full compensation.
body: This is the most discussed apology in Greek literature. Agamemnon says the gods cast 'savage atē' into his mind; he names Zeus, Moira (one's allotted portion, Murray's 'Fate'), and the Erinys 'who walks in mist' (ēerophoitis; Leaf records an ancient variant read as 'blood-drinking'). E. R. Dodds made this passage the starting point of The Greeks and the Irrational: Agamemnon is not dodging responsibility, since he still pays (19.137-8), but describing an experience of sudden, inexplicable folly in the only language available, as an intrusion from outside. Scholars speak here of 'double motivation': an act can be fully the agent's and fully the gods' at once. Others read the speech more cynically, as a king saving face before the army; Achilles himself repeats the explanation (19.270-4), which gives it weight. Leaf notes that the Erinys also brings atē in Od. 15.233-4.

sources.cite: E. R. Dodds, The Greeks and the Irrational (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1951), ch. 1, 'Agamemnon's Apology'
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 19.86-90
Malcolm Davies, 'Agamemnon's apology and the unity of the Iliad', Classical Quarterly 45 (1995), 1-8

anchor: Eldest daughter of Zeus is Ate
title: Atē, the goddess of blindness
greek: Ἄτη (Atē); ἀάομαι (aaomai), 'to be blinded, deluded'
short: Atē, delusion that leads to ruin, is personified as Zeus' eldest daughter, light-footed, walking unseen over men's heads.
body: Atē means both the infatuation that clouds judgement and the ruin that follows; Murray renders it 'blindness'. Here it becomes a goddess: Zeus' eldest daughter, with soft feet that never touch the ground because she walks on men's heads. Leaf takes the image as expressing a silent, mysterious affliction from above, and notes the close parallel with Phoenix's allegory of the Prayers (Litai), the lame daughters of Zeus who follow behind Atē (9.502-12). Plato quotes 19.92-3 in the Symposium (195d) to show the delicacy of Eros, an indication, Leaf remarks, that no one in his day doubted Homer's authorship. Hesiod gives a different genealogy, making Atē a child of Strife (Theogony 230). Agamemnon's use of the figure is self-serving, but the poem endorses the idea elsewhere, and Achilles echoes it at 19.270-4.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 19.88, 19.91 and 19.92
Hesiod, Theogony 230; Plato, Symposium 195d
Liddell-Scott-Jones, Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. ἄτη

title: The birth of Heracles and Eurystheus
greek: Ἀλκμήνη … ἐυστεφάνῳ ἐνὶ Θήβῃ (Alkmēnē … eustephanōi eni Thēbēi)
short: Agamemnon's mythical example: even Zeus was blinded by Atē, when Hera tricked him into an oath that gave Eurystheus power over Heracles.
body: Zeus boasts that a man of his blood born that day will rule all around; Hera makes him swear to it, then hurries to Argos, brings on the seven-month birth of Eurystheus (grandson of Perseus, and so also of Zeus' line), and holds back the Eileithyiai, goddesses of childbirth, from Alcmene. Heracles is thus doomed to labour for Eurystheus. Apollodorus tells the same story (Library 2.4.5), and Ovid adds the trick of Galanthis (Metamorphoses 9.281-323). The tale is a paradeigma: if Zeus himself could be blinded, Agamemnon's error is pardonable. Leaf thought it was adapted from an older Heracles poem, and Davies discusses the 'oddities' that ancient and analytic critics found in it. 'Fair-crowned' (eustephanos) Thebes refers, as Leaf explains, to the city's crown of walls.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), Introduction to Book XIX, p. 318, and notes on 19.99, 19.105, 19.119
Apollodorus, Library 2.4.5
Malcolm Davies, 'Agamemnon's apology and the unity of the Iliad', Classical Quarterly 45 (1995), 1-8 (with reference to M. W. Edwards, The Iliad: A Commentary, vol. 5, on 19.95-133)

anchor: seized Ate by her bright-tressed head
title: Zeus hurls Atē from Olympus
greek: ἕλ᾽ Ἄτην κεφαλῆς λιπαροπλοκάμοιο (hel’ Atēn kephalēs liparoplokamoio)
short: In anger Zeus seizes Atē by the hair and flings her from heaven, which explains why delusion now lives among men.
body: The punishment is an aetiology: Atē, banished from Olympus by an oath, comes down to 'the tilled fields of men', and that is why mortals suffer from her. The violent gesture recalls Zeus hurling Hephaestus from heaven (1.590-4) and his threat to throw any disobedient god into Tartarus (8.10-16). The epithet 'bright-tressed' (liparoplokamos) is unusual and has no parallel in the Iliad; Leaf takes it to refer to hair glossy with oil, and records a scholion explaining that Zeus seized her by the head because she walks on heads. Zeus' groaning whenever he saw Heracles labouring for Eurystheus gives the god a moment of human regret. Agamemnon then applies the story to himself (19.134-6), and Achilles takes up the same idea of god-sent blindness after the oath (19.270-4), so that both parties accept the explanation.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 19.126

title: Food and fasting: Odysseus against Achilles
greek: νήστιας (nēstias), 'fasting'
short: Odysseus insists the army must eat before fighting; Achilles refuses food until Patroclus is avenged. The quarrel over a meal shapes the book.
body: Odysseus' argument is practical: no man can fight all day without food and wine, and the dead must be buried with one day's mourning while the living eat (19.155-72, 225-33). Achilles answers that his heart is set on 'slaying, and blood, and the groanings of men' and that no food will pass his throat (19.199-214). Leaf found this long debate prosaic and a sign of late composition. Many later readers see it instead as thematic: refusing food marks Achilles' withdrawal from ordinary human life and fellowship, so that Zeus must have Athena drip nectar and ambrosia into him (19.340-54). The theme is resolved only in Book XXIV, when Achilles persuades Priam to eat with him, citing Niobe who ate even after losing her children (24.601-20). Odysseus' concern with the belly anticipates his role in the Odyssey.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), Introduction to Book XIX, pp. 317-18

anchor: his feet turned toward the door
title: The corpse laid out feet to the door
greek: ἀνὰ πρόθυρον τετραμμένος (ana prothuron tetrammenos)
short: Patroclus lies with his feet toward the door, the ancient position of a corpse awaiting its carrying-out.
body: The detail records a widespread funeral custom. Leaf compares Persius 3.105, where the dead man stretches his stiff heels toward the door, and Pliny, Natural History 7.46, who says that by nature's rite men are carried out feet first. He suggests the practice arose from a belief that a corpse so placed would find it harder to return as a ghost, citing Erwin Rohde's Psyche and a scholion explaining that those leaving human life should not turn back to the house. In Homer the laying-out (prothesis) is part of a formal sequence of washing, anointing, dressing and lament, which Book XVIII has already begun for Patroclus (18.343-55). Achilles' mention of the position here gives his refusal to eat an image of immediacy: the body is lying in his hut as he speaks.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 19.212 (citing Persius 3.105, Pliny NH 7.46, Rohde, Psyche)

anchor: streweth most straw upon the ground
title: Battle as a harvest with no grain
greek: καλάμην μὲν πλείστην … ἄμητος δ᾽ ὀλίγιστος (kalamēn men pleistēn … amētos d’ oligistos)
short: Odysseus compares battle to a harvest where the bronze cuts down much straw but the yield is tiny: much killing, little gain.
body: Men quickly have their fill of battle, says Odysseus, because in it the bronze strews the most stalks (kalamē) on the ground while the harvest (amētos) is smallest. Leaf glosses the comparison: battle is hard work with little reward, like a farmer who reaps abundant straw and finds little grain, the slaughter being likened to the cutting of the stalks. He quotes Monro's description of it as an ironical understatement, a harvest that is all cutting down and no storing up. The close of the image, 'when Zeus inclines his balance, he who is for men the steward (tamiēs) of war', recalls the scales of Zeus (8.69-72, later 22.209-13); Leaf notes a possible play on the stewards of bread mentioned at 19.44. The metaphor of men as stalks or crops recurs in the reaper simile of 11.67-71.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 19.221-224 (quoting D. B. Monro)

title: The gifts of compensation and the ten talents
greek: ἑπτὰ τρίποδας … χρυσοῦ δὲ στήσας … δέκα πάντα τάλαντα (hepta tripodas … chrusou de stēsas … deka panta talanta)
short: Agamemnon's gifts, first offered in Book IX, are now carried out in public: tripods, cauldrons, horses, women, Briseis, and ten talents of gold.
body: The list repeats Agamemnon's offer in the Embassy (9.122-34). Odysseus insists that the gifts be displayed in the assembly so that everyone sees the restitution (19.172-4): compensation in Homeric society is public, a restoration of honour (timē) as much as of goods. Leaf notes that 'the word said and the deed fulfilled' (19.242) is a proverbial phrase, paralleled in the Hymn to Hermes and Herodotus 3.135. Odysseus weighs out the gold (stēsas, 'setting on the scales'), which, Leaf comments, shows that the Homeric talent was a recognised weight; its actual size is unknown. Briseis comes last as the eighth woman. Achilles, who refused these same gifts in Book IX, now accepts them without interest (19.147-9): what was once the whole issue no longer matters to him.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 19.242, 19.244-5, 19.247

title: The oath sacrifice of the boar
greek: κάπρου ἀπὸ τρίχας ἀρξάμενος (kaprou apo trichas arxamenos)
short: Agamemnon swears on a boar, calling Zeus, Earth, Sun and the Erinyes to witness; the victim is thrown into the sea, not eaten.
body: Agamemnon cuts hairs from the boar's head as 'first-offerings' (aparchai), the same rite as in the oath before the duel of Paris and Menelaus (3.271-301). He invokes Zeus, Earth, the Sun, who sees all things and so can watch an oath, and the Erinyes who punish perjurers under the earth (compare 3.276-9). Leaf notes that competitors at the Olympic games swore on a boar to Zeus Horkios, as Pausanias reports (5.24.9) with a quotation of this passage. The victim of an oath, Leaf observes, is neither burnt nor eaten but devoted to the powers below: here Talthybius whirls it into the sea for the fishes, as in Book III the lambs are carried away. Pausanias says he forgot to ask what was done with the Olympic boar but supposes it was not eaten. The solemnity answers the public charge that Agamemnon had taken Briseis to bed.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 19.197, 19.254, 19.259, 19.267
Pausanias, Description of Greece 5.24.9-11

anchor: Patroclus, dearest to my hapless heart
title: Briseis' lament for Patroclus
greek: Πάτροκλέ μοι δειλῇ πλεῖστον κεχαρισμένε θυμῷ (Patrokle moi deilēi pleiston kecharismene thumōi)
short: Briseis, silent until now, speaks her only lines in the poem: a lament for the one man who was kind to her after her world was destroyed.
body: Briseis' story emerges only here. Achilles killed her husband and her three brothers when he sacked Lyrnessus, the city of Mynes (2.690-3), and Patroclus comforted her by promising that she would become Achilles' lawful wedded wife (kouridiē alochos) with a wedding feast in Phthia. The lament follows the formal pattern of Iliadic laments: address to the dead, contrast of past and present, the speaker's own fate, praise of the dead man ('thou wast ever kind', meilichos). She is compared to golden Aphrodite, and tears her breast, neck and face; Leaf notes that tearing the skin is otherwise unknown among Homeric mourners and wonders whether it is meant as a foreign custom. Leaf, an analyst, judged the speech late on linguistic grounds. Casey Dué has shown how this brief speech draws on a wider tradition of captive women's laments.

sources.cite: Casey Dué, Homeric Variations on a Lament by Briseis (Lanham: Rowman and Littlefield, 2002)
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), Introduction to Book XIX, p. 318, and note on 19.282

title: Mourning Patroclus, weeping for themselves
greek: Πάτροκλον πρόφασιν, σφῶν δ᾽ αὐτῶν κήδε᾽ ἑκάστη (Patroklon prophasin, sphōn d’ autōn kēde’ hekastē)
short: The captive women weep 'with Patroclus as the occasion' but each for her own sorrows; the word prophasis can mean pretext or real cause.
body: This line is often admired as a piece of psychological truth: the enslaved women use the public lament as cover for private grief. The Greek word prophasis usually means 'pretext', but Leaf points out that it can mean simply an avowed or real cause. He records Heyne's objection that the cynical sense is foreign to the poet, and prefers to read the women's grief for Patroclus as genuine, while it awakens deeper sorrows of their own, as with the elders at 19.338-9, who mourn remembering what each left at home, and with the household of Priam at 24.160-8. The same pattern of collective lament in which each mourner grieves her own losses recurs at Achilles' own lament immediately afterwards. Either way, the line lets the voiceless captives of the war, whose cities and husbands the Greeks destroyed, be heard briefly.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 19.262 and 19.302
Liddell-Scott-Jones, Greek-English Lexicon, s.v. πρόφασις

title: Neoptolemus, son of Achilles
greek: Νεοπτόλεμος (Neoptolemos), 'new war'
short: Achilles' son, being raised on Scyros, is named here for the only time in the Iliad; he will later sack Troy.
body: Achilles says that not even news of his father's or his son's death could grieve him more, and names Neoptolemus, raised for him on the island of Scyros. This is the only mention of him by name in the Iliad (compare 24.467). Aristarchus athetized line 327, arguing that Achilles should not be in doubt whether his son lives, since Scyros is near Troy, and that the epithet 'godlike' did not suit a boy; Didymus records a variant giving the name as Pyres, perhaps related to the later name Pyrrhus. Leaf suspected the whole passage, noting that the son plays a leading part in the later epic Cycle but is otherwise unknown to the Iliad. In the Odyssey Odysseus tells Achilles' shade of his son's courage (Od. 11.505-37); in later tradition he kills Priam at the altar (Virgil, Aeneid 2.526-58), a cruel echo of his father's mercy to Priam in Book XXIV.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 19.326-327; Introduction to Book XIX, p. 318
Homer, Odyssey 11.505-37; Virgil, Aeneid 2.526-58

title: Athena swoops like a bird of prey
greek: ἅρπῃ ἐικυῖα τανυπτέρυγι λιγυφώνῳ (harpēi eikuia tanupterugi liguphōnōi)
short: Athena descends to feed the fasting Achilles 'like a harpē, wide of wing and shrill of voice', an unidentified bird of prey.
body: Zeus, pitying Achilles, sends Athena to drop nectar and ambrosia into his breast so that hunger will not weaken him. Her descent is compared to that of a harpē; Murray's 'falcon' is a guess. Leaf says the name presumably marks a bird of prey but that the species cannot be identified, and notes that Aristotle (History of Animals 9) seems to apply it to a sea-bird; he refers readers to D'Arcy Thompson's Glossary of Greek Birds. Homeric gods often move like birds or take bird shape (compare Athena and Apollo as vultures at 7.58-60, Athena as a sea-eagle at Od. 3.371-2), and scholars disagree whether such passages describe transformation or only the speed of flight. The scene underlines the special care of the gods for Achilles at the moment he chooses death.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 19.350
D'Arcy W. Thompson, A Glossary of Greek Birds (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1895), s.v. ἅρπη

title: The snowstorm of helmets and shields
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτε ταρφειαὶ νιφάδες Διὸς ἐκποτέονται (hōs d’ hote tarpheiai niphades Dios ekpoteontai)
short: The Achaeans pour from the ships as thick as snowflakes 'from Zeus' driven by the North Wind; the simile stresses density and brightness.
body: The point of comparison is number and gleam: helmets, bossed shields, plated corslets and ash spears come out of the ships as thick as snow. The flakes are 'of Zeus' (Dios), which Leaf takes as evidence of a primitive sense of Zeus as the sky itself; snow and rain fall from Zeus throughout Homer. Leaf also comments that the verb 'were borne forth' strangely makes the arms the subject instead of the men, quoting Heyne's remark that arms are put for armed men. The snow simile is a favourite Homeric image for multitude: compare the stones flying like snowflakes at 12.278-86. It opens a sequence of light imagery that culminates in the shining arms of Achilles (19.362-83).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 19.357-361

anchor: all the earth round about laughed
title: 'The earth laughed' with the flash of bronze
greek: γέλασσε δὲ πᾶσα περὶ χθών (gelasse de pasa peri chthōn)
short: The whole earth 'laughed' with the gleam of bronze: a metaphor joining shining and laughter, eerily joyful before the slaughter.
body: The verb gelaō normally means 'laugh', but Leaf argues that the ideas of laughing and shining pass naturally into one another, and that the root originally meant 'shine'; the poet probably intends both. He compares Lucretius 2.325-6, where the earth around 'grows bright' (renidescit) with bronze, and Horace, Odes 4.11.6, where the house 'smiles' with silver. The Homeric Hymn to Demeter (13-14) similarly has heaven, earth and sea laugh at the scent of the narcissus. The effect here is unsettling: the landscape seems to rejoice at the very moment Achilles goes out to kill, and the next lines turn at once to the noise of men's feet and to Achilles grinding his teeth.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 19.362 (comparing Lucretius 2.325 and Horace, Odes 4.11.6)
Homeric Hymn to Demeter 13-14

title: Achilles grinds his teeth: the athetesis of 19.365-368
greek: τοῦ καὶ ὀδόντων μὲν καναχὴ πέλε (tou kai odontōn men kanachē pele)
short: Ancient editors questioned these four lines describing Achilles' gnashing teeth and blazing eyes as too undignified for the hero.
body: According to the scholia reported by Leaf, these four lines were athetized (marked as spurious) on the ground that it is ridiculous for Achilles to roar or gnash like a beast, and that the sense runs on without them. Didymus, however, cites Dionysius of Sidon as saying that Aristarchus first obelized the lines and later removed his marks, judging such a description properly poetic; and Leaf notes that Ammonius' account of Aristarchus' second edition says nothing of this. Leaf finds the scholion important as evidence that by Didymus' day the tradition about Aristarchus' views was itself uncertain. Modern readers usually keep the lines: Achilles' bestial fury, like the lion of Book XX (20.164-75), is part of the poem's picture of him, and the eyes 'blazing as with fire' repeat 19.16-17.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 19.365-68 (quoting Schol. A and Didymus)
Homer, Iliad 19.364-68 (Greek)

title: The arming of Achilles (type-scene)
greek: κνημῖδας μὲν πρῶτα περὶ κνήμῃσιν ἔθηκε (knēmidas men prōta peri knēmēisin ethēke)
short: Achilles arms in the fixed order of a Homeric arming scene: greaves, corslet, sword, shield, helmet, spear, here expanded to its grandest form.
body: Arming is one of the Homeric 'type-scenes', with a fixed sequence of lines: greaves, breastplate, sword, shield, helmet, spear. Lines 369-73 repeat the arming of Paris (3.330-5), and the same pattern is used for Agamemnon (11.17-46) and Patroclus (16.130-44). J. I. Armstrong showed that the scenes are not mechanical: each is expanded at significant points, and Achilles' is the most elaborate, with two similes for the gleam of the shield and helmet (19.374-83), the test of fit (384-6) and the Pelian spear, which only he can wield (388-91, repeating 16.140-4, where Patroclus left it behind). Leaf notes that line 374 was suspected by Heyne and Hermann because the shield's gleam is compared twice. The scene's size marks the importance of the moment: Achilles is putting on his death.

sources.cite: J. I. Armstrong, 'The Arming Motif in the Iliad', American Journal of Philology 79 (1958), 337-54
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 19.369-74 and 19.388-91

title: The shield's gleam like a fire seen from the sea
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ἂν ἐκ πόντοιο σέλας ναύτῃσι φανήῃ (hōs d’ hot’ an ek pontoio selas nautēisi phanēēi)
short: The shield's light is like a lonely mountain fire seen by storm-driven sailors far from home: a simile of distance, hope and longing.
body: After comparing the shield to the moon (19.374), the poet adds a second, richer simile: sailors carried by storm winds over the sea, far from their friends, see a fire burning in a lonely farmstead high in the mountains. Leaf explains the basic point as the distance at which a light on a hill can be seen at sea, and suggests a further thought, that Achilles' shining armour cheers his men as a shepherd's fire cheers lost mariners. The detail that they are borne away 'against their will' adds a note of homesickness that echoes Achilles' own situation, far from Phthia and never to return (19.321-37, 421-2). The shield whose gleam is compared here is the one whose decoration, the whole world at peace and war, was described in Book XVIII.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), notes on 19.374 and 19.375

anchor: as it were wings to him
title: The armour like wings
greek: τῷ δ᾽ εὖτε πτερὰ γίγνετ᾽, ἄειρε δὲ ποιμένα λαῶν (tōi d’ eute ptera gignet’, aeire de poimena laōn)
short: Testing the new armour, Achilles finds it so light and well-fitted that it becomes like wings and lifts him up.
body: The god-made armour, instead of weighing Achilles down, seems to raise him. Leaf discusses a textual point that affects the image: the word eute must here mean 'like', 'as it were'. Aristarchus is said to have changed it to aute ('again'), but Leaf argues that this would mean the armour literally became wings again, which cannot be right; the verb 'lifted' itself requires a comparison. Murray's 'as it were wings' follows the reading Leaf defends. The image contrasts with Patroclus, who wore Achilles' old armour and was stripped of it by Apollo (16.791-804), and anticipates the near-divine speed and strength of Achilles in the books that follow.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 19.386

title: The speaking horse Xanthus prophesies Achilles' death
greek: αὐδήεντα δ᾽ ἔθηκε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη (audēenta d’ ethēke thea leukōlenos Hērē)
short: Hera gives the immortal horse Xanthus a human voice: he will save Achilles today, but his death is near, at the hands of 'a god and a mortal'.
body: Achilles rebukes his horses for leaving Patroclus; Xanthus, bowing his head until his mane touches the ground, answers that Apollo, not they, killed Patroclus, and that Achilles is fated to be slain 'by a god and a man' (19.416-17). The prophecy is fulfilled outside the poem but foretold more precisely by the dying Hector: Paris and Apollo will kill him at the Scaean gate (22.359-60). Leaf calls the episode unlike anything else in Homer, but sees no reason to doubt it beyond its uniqueness, comparing the talking animal of Hesiod's fable of the hawk and nightingale (Works and Days 202-12), and praising its restraint. Aristarchus athetized line 407 (Hera's gift of speech) as contradicting line 418, where the Erinyes stop the voice; Leaf thinks lines 407 and 418 were added to soften the miracle. The horses already wept for Patroclus at 17.426-40.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), Introduction to Book XIX, p. 318, and notes on 19.407 and 19.416-17
Hesiod, Works and Days 202-12

title: The Erinyes silence the horse
greek: Ἐρινύες ἔσχεθον αὐδήν (Erinyes eschethon audēn)
short: The Erinyes, usually avengers of wrongs within families and of broken oaths, here stop a horse speaking: guardians of the natural order.
body: Elsewhere in Homer the Erinyes have moral functions: they punish perjury (19.259-60; 3.278-9), enforce the curses of parents (9.454, 571-2), and protect the rights of the elder (15.204). Here they end a breach of nature, the speech of an animal. Leaf comments that they seem to have developed almost into an abstraction of the law that orders the universe, physical as well as moral, and compares Heraclitus' saying (fragment B94 DK, quoted by Plutarch, On Exile 11) that the Sun will not overstep his measures, or the Erinyes, ministers of Justice, will find him out. Leaf thought so refined a conception unlikely in early epic; the scholion's explanation, that all prodigies happen through the Erinyes, shows that ancient readers felt the difficulty too. Achilles' answer (19.420-3) shows him knowingly accepting death.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (1902), note on 19.418
Heraclitus, fragment B94 Diels-Kranz (in Plutarch, De exilio 11, 604a)
